title: The Transformer Deconstructed: How Self-Attention Actually Works Under the Hood
lead: Every modern LLM from GPT-4o to Claude and DeepSeek is built on the Transformer architecture. But behind the jargon of Queries, Keys, and Values lies an elegant, intuitive matrix lookup mechanism.

stats.title: The Scaling Law Revolution:
items: Before Transformers (2017), RNNs and LSTMs were strictly sequential (O(N) time dependency), making training across massive clusters mathematically impossible.
The Transformer's parallel matrix multiplication allowed training compute to scale from thousands of FLOPs to over 10²⁵ FLOPs without vanishing gradients.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: The Filing Cabinet & The Search Query
mentalModel.text:
Imagine a library with millions of file folders:
• Query (Q): What you are searching for right now (the prompt token).
• Key (K): The label on the folder tab (what every other token is about).
• Value (V): The actual content inside the folder.

Self-Attention calculates a dot product between Q and K: It measures how relevant every token is to every other token, generating a weighted average of Values. That's it—no magic, just weighted attention across a semantic coordinate space.

diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Inputs ["Input Embeddings"]
        T["Token: 'Bank'"] --> Q["Query Matrix (Q)"]
        T --> K["Key Matrix (K)"]
        T --> V["Value Matrix (V)"]
    end
    subgraph Attention ["Scaled Dot-Product Attention"]
        Q & K --> MatMul["Q · K^T / sqrt(d_k)"]
        MatMul --> Softmax["Softmax (Attention Weights)"]
        Softmax & V --> Output["Contextual Representation"]
    end
    style Output fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style Softmax fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
codeContent:
import numpy as np

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = np.matmul(Q, K.T) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if mask is not None:
        scores += (mask * -1e9)
    attention_weights = np.exp(scores) / np.sum(np.exp(scores), axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return np.matmul(attention_weights, V), attention_weights

# Q, K, V dimensions: [seq_len, d_k]
output, weights = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q_matrix, K_matrix, V_matrix)

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Attention is a soft, differentiable hash-table lookup across tokens.
Quadratic O(N²) memory complexity in naive attention is why KV-caching and FlashAttention are mandatory in production.
Tokens gain meaning purely from their context: 'Apple' the fruit vs 'Apple' the stock ticker get distinct vectors after layer 1.
takeaway.badge: Every multi-billion parameter model is just stacked blocks of Attention + Feed-Forward layers.

title: Mixture of Experts (MoE): How to Run a 671B Model on the Budget of a 37B Model
lead: Dense models like LLaMA-3 70B activate every single parameter for every single token. Mixture of Experts (MoE) introduces sparse routing, unlocking GPT-4 tier intelligence at 1/10th the inference cost.

stats.title: The Economic Shift to Sparse Architectures:
items: DeepSeek-V3 / Mixtral: DeepSeek-V3 has 671 Billion total parameters, but activates only 37 Billion parameters per token.
MoE models reduce active FLOPs per generated token by up to 75% while maintaining the parametric capacity of a giant model.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: The Hospital Emergency Room Triage
mentalModel.text:
When a patient enters a hospital, you don't assign all 100 specialist doctors to examine their sprained ankle. A triage nurse inspects the symptom and routes the patient to 2 relevant specialists (e.g. Orthopedics and Radiology).

MoE is algorithmic triage: A router network inspects each token and activates only the top-2 most relevant expert feed-forward networks (out of 8, 64, or 256 experts).

diagram:
graph TD
    Token["Input Token Vector"] --> Router["Softmax Gating Router"]
    Router -->|Score: 0.72| Exp1["Expert 2: Code & Logic"]
    Router -->|Score: 0.24| Exp2["Expert 7: Math & Quant"]
    Router -.->|Score: 0.02 (Inactive)| Exp3["Expert 1: Creative Writing"]
    Router -.->|Score: 0.01 (Inactive)| Exp4["Expert 3: Translation"]
    Exp1 & Exp2 --> Aggregator["Weighted Weighted Output"]
    style Exp1 fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style Exp2 fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
    style Exp3 fill:#334155,stroke:#64748b,color:#94a3b8
    style Exp4 fill:#334155,stroke:#64748b,color:#94a3b8
diagramCaption: Figure 2: Sparse Top-K Routing in Mixture of Experts (MoE)
codeContent:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TopKRouter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_experts, top_k=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate = nn.Linear(d_model, num_experts, bias=False)
        self.top_k = top_k

    def forward(self, x):
        logits = self.gate(x) # [batch, seq_len, num_experts]
        weights, indices = torch.topk(F.softmax(logits, dim=-1), self.top_k, dim=-1)
        # Normalize top-k weights to sum to 1.0
        weights = weights / weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        return weights, indices

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: MoE decouples total knowledge capacity (parameter count) from active computation cost (FLOPs).
The primary bottleneck shifts from GPU compute to GPU memory bandwidth (RAM capacity to hold all expert weights).
Load balancing loss is critical during training to prevent router collapse (all tokens routing to expert #1).
takeaway.badge: MoE is why open frontier models now rival proprietary giants at a fraction of the cost.

title: Quantization Deep-Dive: Running 70B Models on a Single GPU with AWQ & GGUF
lead: A 70-Billion parameter model in FP16 precision requires 140GB of VRAM—demanding an expensive dual-A100 server. Quantization compresses weights into INT4/FP8, fitting the exact same model into a single 40GB GPU with under 1% perplexity loss.

stats.title: The Memory Footprint Reality:
items: Standard FP16 = 2 bytes per parameter. A 70B model = 140GB VRAM strictly for weights (excluding KV cache!).
AWQ / INT4 quantization = 0.5 bytes per parameter. That same 70B model shrinks to ~36GB VRAM, running comfortably on a single RTX 6000 or A100.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: High-Resolution FLAC Audio vs. MP3
mentalModel.text:
A studio FLAC audio file captures 24-bit 192kHz audio. But human ears can't perceive 99% of that ultrasonic data. Compressing to a 320kbps MP3 cuts file size by 85% with zero perceivable audio degradation.

Quantization is MP3 compression for neural network weights: Most weights don't need 16 bits of floating-point precision; mapping them into 4-bit integers preserves model intelligence while cutting memory bandwidth by 4x.

diagram:
graph LR subgraph FP16 ["FP16 Precision (16-bit Float)"] F["Weight: 0.142583921...
(16 bits per weight)"] end subgraph INT4 ["INT4 Quantization (4-bit Integer)"] Q["Quantized Bucket: 3
(4 bits per weight)"] end FP16 -->|Activation-aware scaling| INT4 INT4 --> Speed["4x Less Memory Bandwidth
3.5x Higher Token Throughput"] style INT4 fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 3: Floating Point 16-bit to 4-bit Integer Weight Quantization
codeContent:
# Deploying an AWQ Quantized 70B model using vLLM for production throughput
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
    --model Tech-Org/Llama-3-70B-Instruct-AWQ \
    --quantization awq \
    --dtype auto \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
    --max-model-len 8192 \
    --port 8000

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: LLM inference is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Quantization speeds up generation directly by moving 4x fewer bytes across the GPU bus.
Use AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) for server GPUs and vLLM.
Use GGUF / llama.cpp for edge devices, Apple Silicon (Metal), and local desktop deployment.
takeaway.badge: Quantization slashes GPU infrastructure costs by 75% with statistically zero accuracy loss.

audience: AI Engineers & Staff Machine Learning Architects
title: Fine-Tuning Paradigms: Full Fine-Tuning vs. LoRA vs. QLoRA
lead: Should you train every parameter in your foundation model, or freeze the base model and inject low-rank decomposition matrices? Here is the architectural calculus behind parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

stats.title: The GPU Memory Scaling Trap:
items: Full fine-tuning requires holding the model weights, optimizer states (AdamW takes 8 bytes per param!), and gradients in GPU RAM = 16–20 bytes per parameter (~1.4 Terabytes of VRAM for 70B!).
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes base weights and trains < 0.5% of total parameters, reducing training VRAM by 80% with zero catastrophic forgetting.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Transparent Sticky Notes on a Textbook
mentalModel.text:
If you buy an expensive $500 biology textbook, you don't take a sharpie and rewrite every single sentence to add your study notes. You place transparent sticky notes on top of key pages.

LoRA is a transparent sticky note layer: The base model weights W are frozen ($W_0$). We train two tiny low-rank adapter matrices $A$ and $B$ where $\Delta W = B \times A$. During inference, we just add the notes to the base model.

diagram:
graph LR subgraph Frozen ["Frozen Base Model (16-bit)"] W0["W_0: 4096 x 4096 Matrix
(16,777,216 parameters - FROZEN)"] end subgraph LoRA ["LoRA Low-Rank Adapter (Rank r=16)"] A["Matrix A: 4096 x 16
(65,536 params)"] B["Matrix B: 16 x 4096
(65,536 params)"] A --> B end Input["Token Input x"] --> W0 Input --> A W0 & B --> Sum["Output = W_0(x) + (B·A)(x)·(alpha/r)"] style W0 fill:#334155,stroke:#64748b,color:#94a3b8 style B fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 4: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) Architecture Matrix Decomposition
codeContent:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM,
    r=16,               # Rank dimension (typically 8, 16, or 32)
    lora_alpha=32,      # Scaling factor (usually 2x rank)
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj"],
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    bias="none"
)

model = get_peft_model(base_model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# Output: trainable params: 13,631,488 || all params: 8,030,261,248 || trainable%: 0.17%

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Never perform full fine-tuning for domain adaptation; LoRA matches 99% of full fine-tuning performance at a fraction of the cost.
Store multiple LoRA adapters (Customer Support, Code Generation, Legal) and swap them dynamically on a single frozen base model.
QLoRA quantizes the base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) while maintaining 16-bit LoRA adapter gradients.
takeaway.badge: LoRA allows a single foundation model to serve dozens of specialized enterprise tasks simultaneously.

title: From RLHF to DPO & GRPO: The Modern Evolution of Model Alignment
lead: How do you transform an autocomplete token predictor into an aligned, instruction-following assistant? From the complexity of PPO reward models to Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and DeepSeek's Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

stats.title: The Evolution of Post-Training Efficiency:
items: Traditional RLHF with PPO required running 4 separate models in memory simultaneously (Actor, Critic, Reference Model, Reward Model).
DPO and GRPO eliminate the Critic and Reward models, reducing post-training GPU memory overhead by over 50%.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: The Driving Instructor vs. Comparative Grading
mentalModel.text:
• RLHF (PPO): Like having a driving instructor sit next to you scoring your turns in real time with a complex telemetry system.
• DPO: Like a driving test where you are shown two videos of turns: Video A (safe stop) vs. Video B (running a red light). You mathematically increase the probability of Video A and decrease Video B without needing an active driving instructor.

diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph RLHF ["Classical RLHF (PPO) - 4 Models in VRAM"]
        P1["Actor Model"] --> R["Separate Reward Model"]
        P1 --> C["Value/Critic Model"]
        P1 --> Ref["Frozen Reference Model"]
    end
    subgraph DPO ["Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)"]
        Prompt["Prompt x"] --> Win["Preferred Output (y_w)"]
        Prompt --> Lose["Dispreferred Output (y_l)"]
        Win & Lose --> Loss["Closed-form Implicit Reward Loss"]
    end
    style DPO fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 5: RLHF Multi-Model Pipeline vs. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
codeContent:
# Mathematical Representation of DPO Loss:
# L_DPO = -E [ log sigma ( beta * log( pi_theta(y_w|x) / pi_ref(y_w|x) ) 
#                        - beta * log( pi_theta(y_l|x) / pi_ref(y_l|x) ) ) ]
# Optimizes policy directly using preference pairs without training a reward model!

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: DPO has replaced classical PPO in most enterprise post-training pipelines due to stability and memory savings.
GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) benchmarks multiple candidate completions against each other without a separate critic network.
High-quality preference data pairs (Chosen vs. Rejected) are 10x more impactful than raw quantity of generic text.
takeaway.badge: Post-training alignment is where raw intelligence is forged into safe, predictable enterprise behavior.

title: Speculative Decoding: How a Small Draft Model Makes Big LLMs 3x Faster
lead: Autoregressive token generation generates exactly one token per forward pass, bottlenecked entirely by GPU memory latency. Speculative decoding breaks this law: using a tiny 1B draft model to generate candidate tokens in parallel.

stats.title: The Speedup Metrics of Speculative Inference:
items: Speculative decoding achieves 2.2x to 3.4x faster tokens-per-second on 70B models with mathematically identical output.
Zero loss in model accuracy because the large target model runs a single verification pass to accept or reject drafted tokens.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: The Legal Intern Drafting Contracts
mentalModel.text:
A senior law partner reads at 500 words per minute, but dictating a fresh contract word-by-word is agonizingly slow. Instead, a fast junior paralegal drafts 5 sentences. The partner scans all 5 sentences in one second, approves the first 4, and corrects the 5th.

Speculative decoding is the paralegal + partner model: A tiny 1B draft model guesses 5 tokens cheaply; the giant 70B model verifies all 5 tokens in parallel in a single GPU forward pass.

diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Draft as 1B Draft Model (Fast)
    participant Target as 70B Target Model (Accurate)
    participant Client as Output Stream
    
    Draft->>Draft: Generates [T1, T2, T3, T4] (40ms total)
    Draft->>Target: Send 4 candidate tokens
    Note over Target: Parallel Verification Pass (Single GPU step!)
    Target->>Target: Accepts T1, T2, T3. Rejects T4, emits T4_corrected.
    Target-->>Client: Emits 4 verified tokens in the time of 1!
diagramCaption: Figure 6: Draft Generation and Parallel Target Verification
codeContent:
# Launching vLLM with LLaMA-3 70B using LLaMA-3 8B as speculative draft model
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
    --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct \
    --speculative-model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
    --num-speculative-tokens 5 \
    --port 8000

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Speculative decoding delivers free speedups whenever a target model and draft model share the same tokenizer vocabulary.
Ideal for tasks with high predictability (code syntax, JSON schemas, structured data).
Supported natively in modern serving engines: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and TGI.
takeaway.badge: Speculative decoding breaks memory bandwidth bottlenecks without modifying weights.

topic: Hybrid Search: Dense Vectors vs Sparse BM25
title: Why Pure Vector Search Fails: Architecting Hybrid Retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
lead: Vector embeddings capture high-level semantic meaning, but fail miserably at exact keyword matching (SKUs, error codes, part numbers, customer IDs). Here is why every production RAG architecture requires Hybrid Search.

stats.title: The Vector Search Semantic Blindspot:
items: Pure dense vector search retrieval fails up to 43% of the time on exact alphanumeric lookups (e.g. searching for error code 'ERR_AUTH_0921').
Hybrid Search combining Dense Embeddings + BM25 with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) increases Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@10) from 0.61 to 0.89.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Concept Match vs. Phone Book Lookup
mentalModel.text:
• Vector Search: Finds concepts that feel similar. If you search 'heart attack', it finds 'myocardial infarction'.
• BM25 Keyword Search: Finds exact strings. If you search for invoice '#INV-88392-X', it finds that exact invoice, whereas vector embeddings might return '#INV-11029-A' because all invoice numbers have identical embedding vectors!

Hybrid Search fuses both: It searches both indices and combines ranks using Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

diagram:
graph TD Query["User Query: 'Replace error 404 in react router v6'"] --> V["Dense Vector Index
(Cosine Similarity)"] Query --> B["Sparse Lexical Index
(BM25 / Elasticsearch)"] V --> R1["Top 20 Semantic Candidates"] B --> R2["Top 20 Keyword Matches"] R1 & R2 --> RRF["Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
Score = SUM( 1 / (60 + rank) )"] RRF --> Top["Top 5 Unified Context Chunks"] style RRF fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff style Top fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 7: Hybrid Search Architecture with Reciprocal Rank Fusion

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Never deploy pure vector search for enterprise documentation with product codes, IDs, or technical acronyms.
Combine BM25 (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) with Dense Embeddings (pgvector/Pinecone/Qdrant).
Re-rank top hybrid candidates using a Cross-Encoder (Cohere Rerank or BGE-Reranker).
takeaway.badge: Hybrid Search + Reranking is the single highest-ROI upgrade in any enterprise RAG pipeline.

title: PagedAttention & FlashAttention: How Virtual Memory Paging Conquered the KV-Cache
lead: Before vLLM (2023), GPU memory fragmentation wasted up to 80% of VRAM, limiting batch sizes and causing out-of-memory errors on concurrent traffic. Here is how operating system virtual memory solved the LLM serving crisis.

stats.title: The Memory Fragmentation Crisis in LLM Serving:
items: Traditional serving engines pre-allocated contiguous memory blocks for the maximum context window (e.g. 8k tokens), wasting 60%–80% of GPU memory on short prompts.
PagedAttention eliminates external memory fragmentation entirely, boosting concurrent serving throughput by 2x to 4x on identical GPU hardware.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: OS Virtual Memory Pages for KV Cache
mentalModel.text:
In 1960, operating systems stopped allocating contiguous physical RAM for programs; they introduced Virtual Memory Pages and page tables.

PagedAttention brings virtual memory paging to GPUs: The KV-cache for a request is broken into small 16-token blocks stored in non-contiguous GPU memory pages. As new tokens generate, new blocks are dynamically mapped on the fly.

diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Logical ["Logical KV Cache"]
        L1["Tokens 0-15 (Block 0)"]
        L2["Tokens 16-31 (Block 1)"]
        L3["Tokens 32-47 (Block 2)"]
    end
    subgraph Table ["Block Table (Page Table)"]
        T0["Block 0 -> Physical Page #12"]
        T1["Block 1 -> Physical Page #4"]
        T2["Block 2 -> Physical Page #98"]
    end
    subgraph Physical ["Physical GPU VRAM Pages"]
        P4["Page 4 (Non-contiguous)"]
        P12["Page 12"]
        P98["Page 98"]
    end
    Logical --> Table --> Physical
    style Table fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 8: PagedAttention Block Table Mapping to Physical GPU Memory
codeContent:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

# Configure block size and GPU memory utilization
llm = LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
    block_size=16, # Size of each PagedAttention block in tokens
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.90,
    max_model_len=8192
)

prompts = ["Explain Paxos consensus", "Write a quicksort in Rust"]
sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.7, max_tokens=512)
outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Memory fragmentation, not raw compute, is the enemy of high-concurrency LLM deployments.
PagedAttention allows multiple requests to share common prompt prefixes (e.g. system prompts) with zero copy.
FlashAttention optimizes GPU SRAM vs HBM memory transfers to compute attention in O(N) IO complexity.
takeaway.badge: PagedAttention is the foundational breakthrough behind modern enterprise LLM inference engines.

title: Test-Time Compute Scaling: Why Spending More Compute at Inference Wins
lead: For 5 years, scaling laws focused on pre-training (bigger datasets, bigger clusters). Reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) unlocked the new frontier: scaling compute during inference through reinforcement learning.

stats.title: The Inference Scaling Law Breakthrough:
items: On competition math (AIME) and code verification, spending 100x more tokens on reasoning chains boosts accuracy from 16% to over 83%.
Test-time search (MCTS and self-correction rollouts) turns a 7B model into the equivalent of a 70B zero-shot model.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Fast Intuition vs. Deliberate Calculation
mentalModel.text:
• System 1 (Standard LLM): What is 2 + 2? You answer '4' instantly without pausing.
• System 2 (Reasoning LLM): What is 37 × 89? If you blurt out an answer in 50ms, you will fail. You grab pencil and paper, break it into (37 × 80) + (37 × 9), check carrying digits, and verify.

Test-Time compute gives models pencil and paper before emitting the final token.

diagram:
graph TD
    In["Complex Logic Question"] --> CoT["Reasoning Chain (Hidden Test-Time Compute)"]
    CoT --> Check1["Hypothesis A: Fails constraint"]
    CoT --> Check2["Hypothesis B: Backtracks & corrects"]
    CoT --> Valid["Hypothesis C: Verified correct!"]
    Valid --> Out["Clean Final Answer"]
    style CoT fill:#1e3a8a,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style Out fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure: Exploration and Verification Tree during Test-Time Reasoning
codeContent:
# Conceptual Test-Time Rollout & Self-Verification
def test_time_reasoning(model, prompt, num_rollouts=5):
    candidates = [model.generate_thought_chain(prompt) for _ in range(num_rollouts)]
    verified = [c for c in candidates if verify_math_constraints(c)]
    return majority_vote(verified) if verified else candidates[0]

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Inference compute is the new scaling vector when pre-training data hits human text limits.
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (code execution, math proofs) teaches models to self-correct.
Budget your reasoning tokens: simple classification tasks don't need 10,000 reasoning tokens.
takeaway.badge: Test-time compute transforms models from reactive parrots into proactive problem solvers.

title: Flow Matching vs. Diffusion: Why Continuous Normalizing Flows Are Replacing Score-Based Models
lead: Standard diffusion models require 50 to 100 denoising steps through complex stochastic differential equations. Flow Matching straightens probability trajectories, cutting sampling steps by 80% while retaining generative quality.

stats.title: Generative Efficiency Metrics:
items: Optimal Transport Flow Matching achieves parity with standard score-based diffusion in only 10 to 16 Euler steps.
Straight-line trajectories eliminate trajectory curvature, reducing inference latency from 3.2 seconds down to 420 milliseconds on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Curved Drifts vs. Straight Highways
mentalModel.text:
Traditional diffusion pushes random noise particles along curved paths with unpredictable brownian drift. Flow Matching defines a direct velocity vector pointing from pure Gaussian noise directly to the target data distribution.

Straight trajectories allow deterministic numerical ODE solvers to take large, accurate steps without veering off course.

diagram:
graph LR
    Noise["Gaussian Noise Distribution N(0, I)"] --> OT["Optimal Transport Velocity Field"]
    OT --> Step1["Euler Step 1 (t=0.2)"]
    Step1 --> Step2["Euler Step 2 (t=0.6)"]
    Step2 --> Data["Reconstructed Data Distribution (t=1.0)"]
    style Noise fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,color:#fff
    style Data fill:#065f46,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff
diagramCaption: Figure 9: Deterministic Straight-Path Trajectories in Flow Matching
codeContent:
# Minimal Euler Solver for Flow Matching
def flow_matching_sample(model, noise_latents, steps=10):
    dt = 1.0 / steps
    x = noise_latents
    for i in range(steps):
        t = torch.full((x.shape[0],), i * dt, device=x.device)
        velocity = model(x, t)
        x = x + velocity * dt
    return x

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Optimal Transport vectors straighten the generation path between noise and high-fidelity output.
Reduced step counts directly cut real-time serving infrastructure costs.
Deterministic ODE samplers produce predictable, reproducible inference latencies.
takeaway.badge: Flow matching bridges continuous physics and generative AI with predictable sample trajectories.

title: Mamba and Selective State-Space Models: Breaking the Attention Quadratic Bottleneck
lead: Transformer self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, causing memory limits at 128k+ contexts. Selective State-Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba process arbitrary length sequences with linear complexity.

stats.title: Sequence Scaling Benchmarks:
items: Self-attention memory footprints scale O(N^2) as sequence lengths grow beyond 64k tokens.
Selective SSMs maintain a constant-size hidden state, achieving up to 5x higher inference throughput on 100k+ token document processing.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Constant-Size Memory vs. Growing History
mentalModel.text:
A standard Transformer keeps every past token in its KV-cache, demanding more RAM with every token generated. An SSM continuously updates a fixed-size internal state matrix, choosing which signals to remember and which to discard.

Selective scan turns the recurrent state update into an input-dependent filter that trains in parallel and serves in constant memory.

diagram:
graph TD
    Tokens["Input Token Stream x_t"] --> Selective["Selective Scan Gate: B(x), C(x), delta(x)"]
    Selective --> Hidden["Constant Hidden State h_t = A*h_(t-1) + B*x_t"]
    Hidden --> Out["Output Prediction y_t = C*h_t"]
    style Tokens fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,color:#fff
    style Hidden fill:#065f46,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff
codeContent:
# Conceptual Selective Scan Update
def selective_scan_step(h_prev, x_t, A, B_t, C_t, delta_t):
    # Input-dependent discretization
    A_bar = torch.exp(delta_t * A)
    B_bar = delta_t * B_t
    h_next = A_bar * h_prev + B_bar * x_t
    y_t = C_t * h_next
    return h_next, y_t

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Linear time complexity unlocks unbounded sequence context lengths without quadratic memory explosions.
Hardware-aware scan kernels fuse state updates into high-speed SRAM, avoiding GPU DRAM bottlenecks.
Hybrid Transformer-SSM models blend precise recall with linear generation efficiency.
takeaway.badge: Sub-quadratic architectures transform long-context processing from a hardware bottleneck into an engineering reality.

topic: Mixture of Depths (MoD): Dynamic Compute Routing Across Transformer Layers
title: Mixture of Depths: Dynamic Compute Routing Across Transformer Layers
lead: Standard Transformers force every token through every feedforward and self-attention block regardless of difficulty. Mixture of Depths (MoD) dynamically routes trivial tokens around computational blocks via residual bypasses, cutting FLOP consumption by 50% without quality degradation.

stats.title: Dynamic Compute Scaling Metrics:
items: MoD achieves parity with standard dense Transformer baselines using up to 50% fewer FLOPs per token during forward passes.
Fixed capacity routing bounds tensor dimensions, preventing GPU memory fragmentation and maintaining deterministic step latency.

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Express Toll Lanes vs. Local Roads
mentalModel.text:
Every vehicle does not need to navigate crowded downtown streets. Commuters traveling long distances take the high-speed elevated bypass, while vehicles making specific deliveries take local roads.

Mixture of Depths is an express lane for easy tokens: Simple prepositions and punctuation cruise through residual connections, preserving deep matrix multiplications for information-dense nouns, verbs, and logical operators.

    Router --> Cond{"Selected by Top-K?"}
    Cond -- YES --> Block["Execute Transformer Block (Attention + MLP)"]

codeContent:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MixtureOfDepthsRouter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, capacity_factor: float = 0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Linear(d_model, 1, bias=False)
        self.capacity_factor = capacity_factor

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, block_fn):
        # x shape: [batch_size, seq_len, d_model]
        b, s, d = x.shape
        k = int(s * self.capacity_factor)
        router_logits = self.weight(x).squeeze(-1) # [b, s]
        topk_weights, topk_indices = torch.topk(router_logits, k, dim=-1)
        
        # Gather selected tokens for execution
        selected_tokens = torch.gather(x, 1, topk_indices.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, d))
        processed = block_fn(selected_tokens) * torch.sigmoid(topk_weights).unsqueeze(-1)
        
        # Scatter back to residual stream
        out = x.clone()
        out.scatter_add_(1, topk_indices.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, d), processed)
        return out

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Static compute allocations over-spend FLOPs on low-entropy tokens like whitespace, commas, and repetitive syntax.
Capacity factors enforce strict tensor dimensions, avoiding ragged memory allocations on tensor cores.
Combining Mixture of Depths with Mixture of Experts (MoD + MoE) yields compound efficiency gains across both depth and width.
takeaway.badge: Dynamic compute routing transforms fixed Transformer depth into an adaptive, token-dependent computational graph.

topic: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA): Compressing the KV-Cache in DeepSeek V3 and R1
title: Multi-Head Latent Attention: How DeepSeek V3 Shrinks the KV-Cache Bottleneck
lead: Serving 128k context windows on standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) consumes hundreds of gigabytes of GPU VRAM strictly for the KV cache. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) projects Key-Value matrices into a low-rank compressed latent space, reducing cache memory by over 90% while preserving multi-head expressive power.

stats.title: KV-Cache Memory Footprint per Token (671B Model, 128k Context):
items: Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) requires 1,024 bytes per token for Key-Value activations.
Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) reduces KV cache footprint down to 70 bytes per token, achieving a 93.3% memory reduction over MHA and 75% over Grouped-Query Attention (GQA).

mentalModel.title: 1. The 60-Second Mental Model: Compressed MP3 Codecs vs. Uncompressed Audio Stems
mentalModel.text:
Staging uncompressed Multi-Head KV activations in VRAM is like storing raw 32-bit floating point audio tracks for every single choir member on physical high-speed registers. Most of that spectral information is redundant.

MLA compresses the entire chorus into a single low-rank latent vector: The model writes only the compressed latent packet to VRAM, then quickly decompresses the multi-head projection inside high-speed SRAM registers during attention calculation.

    Down --> Latent["Compressed Latent Cache c_t (Stored in VRAM)"]
    Latent --> UpK["Decompress Keys: W_UK"]
    Latent --> UpV["Decompress Values: W_UV"]

codeContent:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class MultiHeadLatentAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, n_heads: int, d_head: int, d_latent: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.d_head = d_head
        # Low-rank KV compression projection
        self.w_dkv = nn.Linear(d_model, d_latent, bias=False)
        # Up-projection decompression matrices
        self.w_uk = nn.Linear(d_latent, n_heads * d_head, bias=False)
        self.w_uv = nn.Linear(d_latent, n_heads * d_head, bias=False)

    def forward_cache_step(self, hidden_state: torch.Tensor):
        # Compress KV to latent representation: shape [batch, 1, d_latent]
        c_kv = self.w_dkv(hidden_state)
        # Only c_kv is stored in GPU KV-Cache VRAM!
        return c_kv

    def compute_attention(self, q: torch.Tensor, c_kv_cache: torch.Tensor):
        # Decompress directly during matrix multiplication
        k = self.w_uk(c_kv_cache).view(q.shape[0], -1, self.n_heads, self.d_head)
        v = self.w_uv(c_kv_cache).view(q.shape[0], -1, self.n_heads, self.d_head)
        return k, v

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Standard GQA reduces key/value heads at the cost of representational fidelity on complex reasoning tasks.
MLA stores low-rank latent representations in VRAM, decompressing heads on-chip without increasing memory bandwidth bottlenecks.
Decoupled RoPE separates rotary positional encodings from the content latent space, preserving relative position awareness.
takeaway.badge: Low-rank latent projection frees frontier models from the memory wall of massive context windows.

topic: Continuous Batching & Chunked Prefill: Eliminating the GPU Bubble in LLM Serving Engines
audience: ML Platform Engineers & High-Throughput Inference Architects
title: Continuous Batching and Chunked Prefill: Maximizing Tensor Core Saturation
lead: Static request batching creates massive GPU compute bubbles while waiting for the slowest token generator to terminate. By transitioning to iteration-level continuous batching and chunked prefill, production inference engines saturate GPU tensor cores and smooth time-to-first-token variance by 4.2x.

items: Static batching leaves tensor cores idling for up to 65% of execution time due to early-finishing request bubbles.
Chunked prefill bounds single-step prefill size to 512 tokens, eliminating decode starvation and reducing P99 latency spikes by 76%.

mentalModel.text:
In a tour bus, all 40 passengers must wait on board until the final passenger boards before the vehicle departs; when one passenger leaves, everyone else sits stalled.

Continuous batching is a baggage carousel: Pieces of luggage (tokens) smoothly drop onto the conveyor belt and leave the carousel the exact moment they finish, keeping the belt moving at maximum linear capacity 100% of the time.

class IterationLevelScheduler:
    def __init__(self, max_batch_tokens: int = 2048, chunk_size: int = 512):
        self.max_batch_tokens = max_batch_tokens
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
        self.prefill_queue = []
        self.decode_pool = []

    def schedule_next_iteration(self):
        current_batch = []
        allocated_tokens = 0
        
        # 1. Prioritize active decodes (1 token per active sequence)
        for req in self.decode_pool:
            current_batch.append((req, 1, "decode"))
            allocated_tokens += 1
            
        # 2. Fill remaining budget with chunked prefill slices
        budget_left = self.max_batch_tokens - allocated_tokens
        for req in list(self.prefill_queue):
            if budget_left <= 0:
                break
            tokens_to_take = min(req.remaining_prefill, self.chunk_size, budget_left)
            current_batch.append((req, tokens_to_take, "prefill_chunk"))
            req.remaining_prefill -= tokens_to_take
            budget_left -= tokens_to_take
            if req.remaining_prefill == 0:
                self.prefill_queue.remove(req)
                self.decode_pool.append(req)
                
        return current_batch

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Static batching is unviable for production LLM serving due to variable generation length disparities.
Chunked prefill prevents long 32k prompt ingestion from blocking real-time token generation for existing users.
Combining iteration scheduling with paged virtual memory enables 3x higher serving density on identical hardware.
takeaway.badge: Iteration-level execution transforms bursty prompt arrivals into continuous, predictable GPU saturation.

topic: Long-Context KV-Cache Compression: StreamingLLM, SnapKV, and Heavy Hitter Eviction
title: StreamingLLM and Heavy-Hitter Eviction: Infinite Context with Bounded Memory
lead: Deploying conversational agents for multi-day streaming tasks quickly exhausts physical GPU memory. Naively dropping early tokens causes perplexity to explode. By preserving critical initial attention sinks alongside rolling local windows and heavy-hitter tokens, models process millions of tokens in constant memory.

Heavy Hitter Oracle (H2O) evicts 80% of intermediate KV positions while preserving over 99.2% accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack evaluations.

An architect does not keep every intermediate draft paper strewn across their working desk. They keep the permanent project charter pinned at the top-left corner (attention sink), the most recent 10 working drawings in front of them (rolling window), and selectively pin 3 critical structural blueprints in the center (heavy hitters).

Attention Sinks stabilize the softmax denominator: Transformers dump unallocated attention probability into the first few tokens. Evicting them ruins attention distributions entirely.

import torch

class StreamingKVCache:
    def __init__(self, n_sinks: int = 4, window_size: int = 512):
        self.n_sinks = n_sinks
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.k_cache = None
        self.v_cache = None

    def update(self, new_k: torch.Tensor, new_v: torch.Tensor):
        if self.k_cache is None:
            self.k_cache, self.v_cache = new_k, new_v
            return self.k_cache, self.v_cache
            
        self.k_cache = torch.cat([self.k_cache, new_k], dim=-2)
        self.v_cache = torch.cat([self.v_cache, new_v], dim=-2)
        
        seq_len = self.k_cache.shape[-2]
        if seq_len > self.n_sinks + self.window_size:
            # Keep initial sinks + recent window, evicting the middle
            sink_k = self.k_cache[:, :, :self.n_sinks, :]
            window_k = self.k_cache[:, :, -self.window_size:, :]
            self.k_cache = torch.cat([sink_k, window_k], dim=-2)
            
            sink_v = self.v_cache[:, :, :self.n_sinks, :]
            window_v = self.v_cache[:, :, -self.window_size:, :]
            self.v_cache = torch.cat([sink_v, window_v], dim=-2)
            
        return self.k_cache, self.v_cache

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: Softmax requires tokens to absorb residual attention mass; the first 4 tokens act as universal sinks.
Pure sliding window attention fails because removing the initial tokens induces catastrophic perplexity surges.
Combining attention sinks with selective eviction allows infinite streaming conversations with bounded constant RAM.
takeaway.badge: Attention sinks turn memory-bounded LLM streaming from a hardware impossibility into a solved problem.

topic: FP8 and Microscaling Formats (MXFP4): Sub-8-Bit Matrix Multiplications on Modern Hardware
audience: Deep Learning Systems Engineers & Hardware Performance Specialists
title: FP8 and Microscaling Formats: Unlocking 2x Compute Density on Modern GPUs
lead: Scaling large language models beyond 100 billion parameters strains memory bandwidth and arithmetic units. Moving from FP16 to FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) and Open Compute Project Microscaling Formats (MXFP4) doubles tensor core throughput while mitigating catastrophic activation outliers.

stats.title: Hardware Throughput & Memory Compression Ratios:

MXFP4 scales small blocks of 32 elements with an independent 8-bit scale factor, preserving numerical dynamic range with 75% memory savings.

A fixed single-speed bicycle forces a rider into a single gear ratio; when encountering a steep mountain, the pedals stall, and on a steep descent, the legs spin uselessly.

Microscaling provides a dynamic micro-gearbox for every 32 numbers: Rather than forcing an entire multi-gigabyte weight matrix into a single fixed range where outliers crush precision, every block of 32 weights gets its own private scale exponent.

import torch

def mxfp4_block_quantize(x: torch.Tensor, block_size: int = 32):
    # Reshape input tensor into micro-blocks of 32 elements
    orig_shape = x.shape
    blocks = x.view(-1, block_size)
    
    # Calculate shared 8-bit scale per block (power-of-two exponent)
    max_abs = blocks.abs().amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-12)
    shared_exp = torch.floor(torch.log2(max_abs))
    shared_scale = 2.0 ** shared_exp
    
    # Normalize blocks by shared exponent
    normalized = blocks / shared_scale
    
    # Quantize to 4-bit representation (e.g. E2M1: 1 sign, 2 exp, 1 mantissa)
    q_blocks = torch.clamp(torch.round(normalized * 6.0), -6.0, 6.0) / 6.0
    dequantized = (q_blocks * shared_scale).view(orig_shape)
    return dequantized, shared_scale

takeaway.title: Key Takeaways
items: E4M3 format is optimal for forward passes and activations due to higher precision; E5M2 is optimal for gradients due to wide dynamic range.
Per-tensor quantization fails in deep networks because activation outliers in residual streams crush small values to zero.
Microscaling formats standardize 32-element tiling directly into silicon, eliminating software quantization dequantization overhead.
takeaway.badge: Hardware microscaling unlocks sub-byte tensor arithmetic without sacrificing representational accuracy.
